title: Quantum computing-based solver for interacting power grids
authors: Ankit Kumar Das, Durgesh Pandey, P. Arumugam
abstract: The proliferation of power electronics in multi-terminal transmission grids has increasingly led to harmonic distortions and dynamic instabilities. While Resonance Mode Analysis (RMA) provides deep insights into these system resonances, evaluating the critical modes of large-scale grids presents a severe computational bottleneck. Classical iterative techniques must continuously diagonalize massively high-dimensional, non-Hermitian admittance matrices across a wide frequency spectrum, a process that rapidly exhausts classical memory and processing limits. To overcome this scaling barrier, we propose a novel quantum-classical hybrid methodology that natively maps the transmission grid's admittance matrix onto a Quantum Processing Unit (QPU). Because the grid's matrix is non-Hermitian, standard quantum eigensolvers are insufficient; thus, we employ the Real Variance-based Variational Quantum Eigensolver (RVVQE) algorithm to accurately extract the complex eigenvalues that represent the system's modes. Validated against a standard 5-bus transmission system, the quantum-derived critical-resonance modal impedances demonstrate near-perfect alignment with the exact classical frequency responses. Crucially, by encoding the grid's state logarithmically into quantum memory, this methodology bypasses classical RAM limitations. The successful implementation of the RVVQE framework not only bridges the mathematical topologies of dissipative electrical grids and open quantum systems but also provides a profoundly scalable architecture capable of diagnosing resonance instabilities in massive, continental-scale networks that currently exceed classical computational boundaries.
summary: The paper introduces a quantum-classical hybrid solver to overcome the computational bottleneck of analyzing resonance instabilities in massive power grids. By adapting the RVVQE algorithm for non-Hermitian matrices, it maps the grid's admittance matrix onto a QPU. This scalable approach promises to diagnose continental-scale electrical network failures currently beyond classical computing limits.
main_problem: Evaluating critical resonance modes of large-scale interacting power grids is computationally intractable for classical methods due to the need to diagonalize massive, non-Hermitian admittance matrices.
main_result: The proposed quantum-classical hybrid methodology successfully extracts critical resonance modal impedances with near-perfect accuracy compared to classical solutions on test systems.
method: A novel Quantum-Classical Hybrid Resonance Mode Analysis (Q-RMA) framework is used, employing the Real Variance-based Variational Quantum Eigensolver (RVVQE) algorithm to handle the non-Hermitian nature of the grid admittance matrix ($\mathbf{Y}_{B,f}$).
model_or_system: The system modeled is a multi-terminal power transmission grid, represented mathematically by its frequency-dependent, non-Hermitian admittance matrix ($\mathbf{Y}_{B,f}$), which governs dynamic instabilities.
key_observables: Critical resonance modal impedances ($Z_{cm,f}$) and eigenvalues of the admittance matrix across a wide frequency spectrum (100 Hz to 3000 Hz).
important_parameters: The size of the grid ($n$-bus system), which dictates the required number of qubits ($\lceil\log_2 nceil$).
main_assumptions: Standard quantum eigensolvers are insufficient because they only handle Hermitian matrices, necessitating the use of RVVQE for the non-Hermitian $\mathbf{Y}_{B,f}$.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the hybrid framework mapping $\mathbf{Y}_{B,f}$ onto a QPU using RVVQE. Figure 2 shows the iterative workflow (Q-RMA) across frequency sweeps. Figure 4 compares quantum RVVQE results against exact classical solutions for $|Z_{cm}|$.
paper_structure: The paper outlines the problem (harmonic distortions in grids), proposes the Q-RMA methodology involving matrix decomposition ($\mathbf{Y}_{B,f} = \mathbf{H}_f + i\mathbf{K}_f$), details the RVVQE implementation for non-Hermitian operators, and validates the approach by comparing quantum results to classical benchmarks.
why_interesting: This work directly applies advanced quantum algorithms (RVVQE) to a complex engineering problem involving open quantum systems dynamics, bridging theoretical quantum computation with large-scale physical infrastructure analysis.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed hybrid quantum-classical framework for resonance mode analysis (RMA) of power transmission grids. The system admittance matrix is decomposed into Hermitian components and solved using the Real Variance-based Variational Quantum Eigensolver (RVVQE) to obtain the eigenvalues and eigenvectors required for resonance and stability analysis.

Fig. 2. Workflow of the proposed hybrid quantum-classical (HQC) framework for resonance mode analysis. The non-Hermitian admittance matrix is decomposed into Hermitian components and mapped to Pauli operators. The RVVQE algorithm iteratively prepares the quantum state, performs QPU measurements, and updates the circuit parameters until convergence, after which the resonance modes are extracted for stability assessment.
Fig. 3. Three-qubit unitary rotation entangled ansatz with nearest-neighbor CNOT gates. The complete rotation for each qubit allows exploration of full Hilbert space spanned by 3 qubits.

Fig. 4. Validation of the quantum algorithmic framework on the 5-bus transmission system. The critical resonance modal impedance (|Zcm|) is plotted across a continuous frequency spectrum. The solid blue line represents the exact classical solution derived via standard matrix diagonalization, while the red markers indicate the eigenvalues computed using the Quantum RVVQE algorithm. The near-perfect overlap confirms the accuracy of the quantum approach in capturing the singularities of the non-Hermitian admittance matrix.
